Neonatal tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) emerge from their mothers as well-developed pups, with parturition typically occurring in warm, subtropical waters. Field surveys of nursery grounds in the North Atlantic indicate that newborns measure approximately 62 centimeters [Lb = approximately 62 centimeters] in total length at birth, although a broader range extending from 51 to 76 centimeters [Lb = 51 to 76 centimeters] has been documented across different populations. The wet weight at birth averages around 929 grams [Wwb = around 929 grams], a modest mass that belies the robust, fast-growing nature of this apex predator. These neonatal values reflect a reproductive strategy that balances relatively large offspring size against substantial litter production, a trade-off common among carcharhinid sharks. Gestation occurs over a protracted period, and the age at birth, under ambient oceanic thermal conditions typical of this species’ range, has been estimated at approximately 503 days [ab = approximately 503 days] when maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a duration that aligns with the slow developmental rates observed in other large-bodied elasmobranchs.

Growth trajectories in tiger sharks exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism, a pattern consistent across many lamniform and carcharhiniform lineages. Adult females ultimately achieve considerably larger asymptotic dimensions than their male counterparts, a disparity linked to the energetic demands of gestation and the need for a spacious body cavity to accommodate developing litters. Extensive mark-recapture studies in the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans have recorded that the ultimate total length for females reaches 550 centimeters [Li = 550 centimeters], while males max out at a substantially smaller 428 centimeters [Li = 428 centimeters]. This difference in maximum size is reflected in the corresponding ultimate wet weights, which have been derived from length-weight regressions specific to the species; females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1,144 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 1,144 kilograms], in contrast to the 505 kilograms [Wwi = 505 kilograms] recorded for males. Such pronounced sexual size dimorphism is thought to confer reproductive advantages on larger females, including higher fecundity and enhanced offspring survival.

The onset of puberty in tiger sharks is tightly linked to body size rather than strictly to chronological age, a common pattern in elasmobranchs where somatic growth rates are highly variable. Analyses of gonadal development in specimens collected from the Gulf of Mexico and the western Indian Ocean indicate that females reach sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 300 centimeters [Lp = approximately 300 centimeters], whereas males become reproductively mature at a smaller size of 250 centimeters [Lp = 250 centimeters]. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty for females has been calculated as 159 kilograms [Wwp = 159 kilograms], while males achieve puberty at a wet weight of 87.5 kilograms [Wwp = 87.5 kilograms]. The time since birth at puberty is estimated at roughly 7 years [tp = roughly 7 years] under a stable thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. Reproductive output in Galeocerdo cuvier is characterized by large litters and a relatively slow reproductive cycle, a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring size and quality over rapid generational turnover. Dissections of gravid females have consistently revealed that a single litter comprises between 10 and 18 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 10 and 18 pups per litter], and the frequency of reproductive events is approximately one pupping event every 3 years [Ri = approximately one pupping event every 3 years], a long interval that reflects the energetic cost of gestation and the subsequent period of somatic recovery. When considered under a stabilized thermal context at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], this combination of litter size and inter-birth interval defines the species’ maximum reproductive rate. This low fecundity relative to body size, alongside late maturity, underscores the tiger shark’s classification as a K-selected species particularly sensitive to fishing pressure. Populations in heavily exploited regions have shown slow recovery rates, prompting conservation concerns.

Longevity represents a critical parameter for understanding population dynamics and extinction risk in long-lived marine predators. The maximum lifespan of the tiger shark, based on vertebral band counts and mark-recapture data, has been estimated at approximately 27.3 years [am = approximately 27.3 years] under a constant water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a value consistent with the AnAge database entry of 25 years for this species. This extended lifespan, combined with late maturity and infrequent reproduction, results in a long generation time that slows the intrinsic rate of population increase. Tiger sharks are also known for their relatively high basal metabolic demands, which scale with their large body size and active predatory lifestyle. Their ecological role as a wide-ranging apex predator, capable of traversing entire ocean basins, further influences their life-history evolution. Comparative analyses with other carcharhinid sharks suggest that the tiger shark’s combination of moderate longevity and high fecundity provides a demographic buffer against environmental stochasticity, though not against sustained anthropogenic mortality.
